newsitem.title: BELARUS: Lukashenko says TV misrepresents Belarus clashes.
newsitem.headline: Lukashenko says TV misrepresents Belarus clashes.

text.p: Belarussian President Alexander Lukashenko on Wednesday accused television stations of misrepresenting clashes between protesters and police during recent opposition rallies in his former Soviet republic.

"On television they showed a woman being beaten, then it turned out it was a Japanese man. But no one apologised," he told officials as he surveyed the spring sowing campaign at a collective farm at the village of Khidry in western Belarus.
"There is none of that craziness shown on the television. A picture is made in advance. A proviso is set of showing a dictatorship," he said.
Belarussian authorities have cracked down hard on opposition protests in the capital Minsk against Lukashenko's rule and his policy of forming a union with Russia.
When he signed a Union Treaty with Russian President Boris Yeltsin in Moscow on April 2, protesters tried to march on the Russian embassy in Minsk but their protest ended in violence.

Police blocked their way and then waded into the crowd as some protesters started throwing stones. Reuters correspondents at the scene saw riot police with shields and helmets and ordinary police with truncheons beat protesters.

"In Minsk 1,500 or 2,000 people gather and then western and Russian media talk about human rights violations. We would never have set ourselves the goal of beating anyone up. I, as head of state, and structures below me are obliged to defend this embassy," Lukashenko said.
The Belarussian leadership has suffered a barrage of criticism from European institutions and Washington for its civil rights record but Lukashenko was unrepentant on Wednesday.
"We don't need to be taught democracy," he said.

Lukashenko, in a bid to avert a "Belarus Spring" of opposition protests, has clamped down on marches in the capital and scores of top opposition figures have been detained for taking part in banned demonstrations.
Journalists have also been arrested and beaten at protests and Russian NTV's correspondent was deported for alleged bias.
Lukashenko was clearly irritated by plans to hold another mass meeting on April 26, the 11th anniversary of the Chernobyl disaster which affected much of Europe but Belarus worst of all.
Perhaps mindful of clashes which erupted at a similar meeting last year, he suggested protesters should travel to the 30-km (17-mile) restricted "zone" around Chernobyl in neighbouring Ukraine.
"It would be better to hold the Chernobyl demonstration in the 30-km zone. You don't need to be very clever to take a walk through clean, well-tended Minsk," he said.
Lukashenko made clear he would not budge from his position of uniting with Russia while maintaining sovereignty.
Belarus was not looking towards NATO, unlike its neighbours which want to be part of the eastwards expansion of the western military alliance, he said.

"Belarus must firmly determine today who she will be with. NATO means the integration of Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary, the Baltic republics. The question is, are we Belarussians with NATO or with Russia. Not a single Belarussian has told me to go to NATO," he said.
Lukashenko enjoys broad popular support in Belarus but is actively opposed by a loose union of nationalists, liberals, intellectuals and students concentrated mostly in the capital.
Nationalists often hold banners reading "Belarus into NATO".
